title: The Next Trillion-Dollar Company No Longer Selling You Software. It Will Sell You the Work
author: GL

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI should drive work and business-model redesign and that governance is essential, but redirects the cluster’s human-led, selective-copilot framing toward AI-native providers delivering bounded categories of work on an autopilot basis. It qualifies this by retaining some human involvement, yet its claims that autopilot-native firms will prevail and outsourced legal work is broadly addressable are predictions rather than task-level evidence of reliable autonomy.
qs: The more powerful question is: which categories of work in your organization are already, or could soon be, fully delivered by an AI agent team?
Not because you should eliminate every human, but because the work that is already accepted as deliverable externally is precisely the work most ready for AI-native delivery.

st.t: Agentic infrastructure: Harvey tests vertical vendor durability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between copilot tools and AI-native providers delivering legal work, then materially extends it with a customer-incentive mechanism: vendors serving hourly-billing firms may be constrained from replacing the human work their customers monetize. It also identifies outsourced professional-services spending as the addressable market for autopilot providers. Its prediction that autopilot-native firms will win is more categorical than the cluster’s deliberately uncertain assessment.
qs: The copilot company is structurally captured by the interests of its current client base.

Wherever you currently spend money on outsourced professional services — legal work, compliance reviews, financial processing, research, communications — that spend represents an addressable autopilot opportunity.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s operating-model and bargaining-shift thesis, then materially extends it by arguing that incumbent law-firm incentives constrain copilot vendors while AI-native autopilot providers can target work currently outsourced to professional-service providers. Its claim that autopilot-native firms will win is a forecast rather than evidence of a completed market shift.
qs: A law firm that has invested in Harvey as a productivity tool has no interest in seeing Harvey replace the billable hours that tool was meant to protect.

Wherever you currently spend money on outsourced professional services — legal work, compliance reviews, financial processing, research, communications — that spend represents an addressable autopilot opportunity.

kp.k: AI services target work budgets rather than software budgets
kp.d: GL endorses Sequoia partner Julien Bek’s March 5, 2026 thesis that the next trillion-dollar company will sell completed work rather than tools. The proposed mechanism is that service providers capture existing professional-services spending and benefit from improving models through faster, cheaper delivery and expanding margins, whereas tool vendors face intensified model competition. This is a business-model prediction, not a demonstrated valuation outcome.
qs: Its central claim: the next trillion-dollar company will not sell you a software tool. It will sell you the actual work that tool was meant to help you do.
$6 spent on services for every $1 spent on software.
But when you sell the work, every model improvement is a competitive advantage. Your margins expand. Your delivery accelerates. Your pricing becomes more attractive.

kp.k: Copilots augment professionals; autopilots replace defined intermediary functions
kp.d: Reporting Bek’s framework, GL distinguishes software that assists an accountable human expert from services delivering a defined outcome directly to the buyer. Harvey and Rogo illustrate the copilot model, while Crosby and With Coverage illustrate the autopilot model. The substitution claim concerns defined categories of work rather than the elimination of every professional.
qs: The expert remains the customer. The expert takes responsibility for the output. Harvey sells to law firms. Rogo sells to investment banks.
It removes the need for that expert intermediary entirely, for a defined category of work.
The customer is buying the outcome. The transaction is complete without the human professional layer.

kp.k: Direct legal delivery competes for corporate legal spending
kp.d: GL presents Crosby’s NDA delivery as a legal-services example of selling outcomes directly to corporate buyers rather than selling software to law firms. The argument is that this changes the addressable budget from law-firm technology expenditure to companies’ legal spending. The document describes this commercial positioning without supplying transaction volumes, pricing or legal-quality measurements.
qs: Crosby drafts your NDA and delivers it directly to you — no outside counsel required.
Crosby does not sell to law firms. It sells to the company that needs an NDA drafted.
Legal SaaS companies compete for a fraction of law firm revenues. Crosby competes for a fraction of every company’s legal spend.

kp.k: Existing outsourcing creates an entry route for AI-native providers
kp.d: GL attributes to Bek the argument that externally purchased, outcome-based work offers an easier market entry because buyers already accept external delivery and have allocated budgets. Legal contract work, tax advisory, IT management, procurement and hiring are presented as a combined multi-trillion-dollar opportunity. GL recommends that executives map outsourced legal work, compliance, processing, research and communications as potential agent-delivered services.
qs: Legal contract work, tax advisory, IT management, supply chain procurement, hiring: a combined multi-trillion-dollar market, all characterized by outsourced, outcome-based work that buyers already purchase externally.
The transition from outsourced human provider to AI-powered service firm is, as Bek notes, a supplier change — not a cultural revolution.

Wherever you currently spend money on outsourced professional services — legal work, compliance reviews, financial processing, research, communications — that spend represents an addressable autopilot opportunity.

kp.k: Labour shortages strengthen the cross-sector automation argument
kp.d: In its account of Bek’s opportunity map, the article reports an $80 billion US accounting and audit market, 340,000 accountants leaving over five years, $50–80 billion in outsourced US healthcare revenue-cycle work, and $50–80 billion in insurance claims adjusting. It treats workforce shortages and aging personnel as reasons AI intervention is becoming necessary; these are reported sector claims rather than evidence about lawyer employment.
qs: Accounting and audit: an $80 billion market in the US alone, currently hemorrhaging talent — 340,000 accountants have left the profession over five years with no replacement pipeline.
Healthcare revenue cycle: $50–80 billion outsourced in the US.
Insurance claims adjusting: $50–80 billion, with an aging adjuster workforce and no succession plan in sight.

kp.k: Insurance and healthcare illustrate outcome-delivery mechanisms
kp.d: GL describes WithCoverage as delivering insurance directly to CFOs and capturing the broker’s margin without its overhead. It reports Bek’s characterization of Anterior as an advanced healthcare-coding autopilot, involving translation of clinical notes into approximately 70,000 ICD-10 codes. Claims that Anterior is faster, more accurate and cheaper are asserted without accompanying comparative measurements.
qs: The company delivers a complete outcome — coverage arranged, policy issued — through an AI-native service layer.
The broker’s margin becomes With Coverage’s margin, captured without the broker’s overhead.
Medical coding translates clinical notes into approximately 70,000 standardized ICD-10 codes — complex rules, but rules nonetheless.
Anterior just does it faster, more accurately, and at lower cost.

kp.k: Agent market forecasts underpin the service-growth thesis
kp.d: The article cites Grand View Research’s 2025 forecast of 46.3% CAGR, from $7.84B in 2025 to $52.62B by 2030, and Gartner’s forecast that 40% of enterprise applications will include task-specific agents by end-2026, versus under 5% the prior year. It separately reports a 2025 market exceeding $7.6 billion and some 2033 estimates of $183 billion. GL distinguishes agent infrastructure revenue from the service revenue providers might generate with agents; the future figures are projections.
qs: 46.3% CAGR for the AI agents market, growing from $7.84B in 2025 to $52.62B by 2030.
40% of enterprise applications will include task-specific AI agents by end of 2026, up from under 5% last year.
The AI agents market crossed $7.6 billion in 2025.
By 2033, some estimates reach $183 billion.
And this is purely the agent infrastructure market — not the service revenue those agents will generate on behalf of the firms, like Human Haus, who deploy them.

kp.k: Reported enterprise adoption and returns support commercial expectations
kp.d: GL cites the 2025 PwC Business Leaders Survey for 79% reporting some agentic AI adoption and 96% planning expansion, the 2025 Landbase/PwC Agentic AI Report for reported average ROI of 171% and US enterprise ROI of 192%, and a 2025 IDC survey for over 80% reconsidering packaged applications. These are reported survey findings and intentions, not legal-sector-specific performance results; no sample sizes or methods are supplied.
qs: 79% of enterprises report some level of agentic AI adoption, with 96% planning to expand usage.
171% average ROI reported by companies deploying agentic AI — US enterprises reporting 192%.
80%+ of organizations say AI agents are “the new enterprise apps” triggering reconsideration of packaged app investments.

kp.k: Adoption-to-scale gap creates demand for deployment services
kp.d: The article reports McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI survey as finding 88% of organizations using AI in at least one function but fewer than 10% successfully scaling it across operations. GL interprets this gap as a deployment and design problem rather than a technology problem, and as the opportunity for Agents as a Service firms. That causal interpretation belongs to GL rather than being identified as a McKinsey finding.
qs: McKinsey’s 2025 State of AI survey found that while 88% of organizations now use AI in at least one function, fewer than 10% have successfully scaled it across their operations.
This gap between adoption and transformation is not a technology problem. It is a deployment and design problem.
It is precisely the problem that Agents as a Service firms exist to solve.

kp.k: Copilot vendors face customer conflicts when replacing legal work
kp.d: GL attributes an innovator’s-dilemma argument to Bek: vendors such as Harvey and Rogo would compete with their existing professional customers if they shifted from assisting them to delivering their work directly. GL frames law-firm protection of billable hours as a structural obstacle and predicts an advantage for providers founded as autopilots. The article reports Bek’s expectation that many copilots will attempt the transition in 2026 and that native autopilots will win.
qs: But selling the work means cutting their existing customers out of doing it.
A law firm that has invested in Harvey as a productivity tool has no interest in seeing Harvey replace the billable hours that tool was meant to protect.
The copilot company is structurally captured by the interests of its current client base.
In 2025, the fastest-growing AI companies were copilots. In 2026, many will try to become autopilots. Bek’s verdict is unambiguous: the ones that started as autopilots will win.

kp.k: Governance and oversight are proposed competitive advantages
kp.d: GL reports a Gartner warning that over 40% of agentic AI projects risk cancellation by 2027 because of inadequate governance and risk controls. Later, GL describes this as a projected 40% failure rate and categorically attributes future failures to governance rather than technology. The article recommends foundational accountability, oversight and ethical safeguards, predicting that well-governed providers will gain clients from unsuccessful competitors.
qs: As Gartner has already warned, over 40% of agentic AI projects are at risk of cancellation by 2027 due to inadequate governance and risk controls.

The 40% project failure rate that Gartner projects for agentic AI by 2027 will not be caused by technology failures. It will be caused by governance failures — unclear accountability, absent oversight frameworks, and ethical blind spots discovered too late.
The organizations and service firms that build governance into their agent architectures from the foundation will not just avoid failure. They will inherit the clients of everyone who did not.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: GL argues that AI-native service firms will sell completed professional work rather than software, replacing expert intermediaries for defined tasks and capturing clients' service budgets.
pts.d: GL endorses and extends the thesis discussed in Sequoia's essay: copilots augment professionals who remain responsible for output, whereas autopilots deliver outcomes directly to buyers. In legal services, GL contrasts Harvey, a software supplier to law firms, with Crosby, described as directly supplying NDA drafting to companies without outside counsel. GL argues that selling work targets a larger spending pool than selling software, that model improvements compound service providers' cost and margin advantages, and that the next trillion-dollar company will follow this model. These are GL's adopted claims and predictions, not independently established findings in this article. The substitution claim concerns defined categories of work, not the disappearance of all lawyers.

pts.k: GL predicts that providers founded to deliver autonomous services have a structural advantage over copilot vendors whose existing professional customers resist replacement.
pts.d: GL argues that Harvey and comparable copilot companies face customer conflicts if they begin delivering the work their customers currently bill for. Firms that start as direct service providers allegedly avoid this constraint. GL also describes existing outsourcing relationships as a ready route to market: replacing a human provider with an AI-native provider is characterized as a supplier change rather than a fundamental change in purchasing behavior. The source presents first-mover trust, methodology and client relationships as important advantages.

pts.k: Across professional services, GL claims that agent teams can deliver outcomes directly, while governance and deployment design will determine which providers scale.
pts.d: GL describes WithCoverage as arranging insurance directly for CFOs without brokers and Anterior as delivering healthcare coding faster, more accurately and more cheaply. GL presents Human Haus as already deploying autonomous agent teams for defined professional work. The article interprets the gap between widespread AI use and limited organizational scaling as a deployment-and-design problem, rather than a technology problem. It predicts that governance failures will drive agent-project cancellations and that providers with foundational oversight and accountability will gain competitors' clients. Human Haus's six-phase methodology, human oversight and legal-industry roots are presented as competitive advantages; no outcome measurements for that methodology are supplied.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: GL supports the thesis with attributed market estimates and surveys, named company illustrations, Sequoia's authority and Human Haus's account of its own business.
pts.d: The article cites Sequoia for a six-to-one services/software spending ratio and sector opportunities, including an $80 billion US accounting-and-audit market, 340,000 accountants leaving over five years, and $50–80 billion each in healthcare revenue-cycle outsourcing and insurance claims adjusting. It cites Grand View Research for agent-market growth forecasts, Gartner for enterprise-agent penetration, PwC for adoption intentions, Landbase/PwC for reported ROI, McKinsey for the adoption/scaling gap, and IDC for reconsideration of packaged applications. Crosby, WithCoverage and Anterior are illustrative cases, not comparative performance studies presented in the document. The article supplies no legal-task benchmark, measured legal-service outcomes or quantified Human Haus results. Its evidence includes both reported survey findings and forward-looking estimates; these are not the same as demonstrated future outcomes. GL's own commercial involvement is explicit.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Writing on 11 March 2026, GL portrays the shift as underway, expects competitive repositioning during 2026, and cites forecasts through 2027, 2030 and 2033.
pts.d: The company examples and Human Haus activity are presented as current. GL expects copilot-to-autopilot transitions in 2026 and describes the first-mover window as open but temporary, without specifying its closing date. The article cites Gartner's forecast of 40% enterprise-application agent inclusion by the end of 2026 and initially describes more than 40% of agentic projects as at risk of cancellation by 2027; later it calls this a projected 40% failure rate caused by governance failures. Agent-market forecasts extend to roughly $50 billion by 2030 and, in some unnamed estimates, $183 billion by 2033. No date is supplied for the trillion-dollar-company prediction. Favorable conditions include defined work categories, existing outsourcing budgets, outcome-based purchasing, continued model improvement and governance designed in from the outset. Although GL describes removal of expert intermediaries, it also explicitly qualifies the opportunity as not requiring elimination of every human and emphasizes human oversight.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate buyers, professional intermediaries, copilot software vendors and AI-native service providers across outsourced professional work.
pts.d: Companies buying legal contract work, including NDAs, are described as able to purchase completed outcomes directly rather than engage outside counsel for those tasks. Law firms and lawyers face potential loss of intermediary work and associated billable hours; Harvey is discussed as a vendor exposed to conflict with its law-firm customers, not as an existing autonomous legal-service provider. AI-native providers such as Crosby and Human Haus are positioned to capture service or labor spending rather than software-seat spending. In other domains, CFOs may buy coverage without brokers, and healthcare coding, accounting, claims adjusting, tax advisory, IT management, procurement and hiring are identified as opportunities. Business owners, executives and strategists are urged to reconsider outsourced work categories and governance. The article does not specify effects on associate staffing structures, individual access to justice or the distribution of employment losses.
